W7221518369.abstract: Abstract Command and control (C2) is an agile crisis management architecture for highly uncertain emergencies, originating from military operations but now widely deployed in public safety emergency response, traffic and airspace management, industrial energy systems, urban governance, and large-scale event coordination. Traditional C2 systems mainly rely on preset rules, static processes and manual decision-making, which expose obvious limitations in the face of modern environments with high dynamics, complex disturbances and incomplete information. Aiming at the significant problems of traditional command and control systems, such as structural rigidity, information overload, decision lag, and insufficient collaboration, based on the concepts of software factory and single-agent factory, combined with the latest progress of large-small model collaboration in the field of command and control, this paper proposes a new paradigm of large-small model collaboration empowering command and control—the concept of C2 multi-agent factory, which upgrades the single-agent factory that produces “individual intelligence” to a multi-agent factory that produces and runs “swarm intelligence”, and is combined with the command and control system and its application scenarios. The overall system architecture of the C2 multi-agent factory and the large-small model collaboration mechanism based on the C2 multi-agent factory are given. Finally, an application example is given to further illustrate how the C2 multi-agent factory can use the large-small model collaboration technology to empower command and control. The C2 multi-agent factory proposed in this paper will find a new path for the construction of an evolvable intelligent command and control system, promote the substantive leap of artificial intelligence towards the C2 system.

W7221533683.abstract: Lead-free double perovskite solar cells (DPSCs) have emerged as attractive alternatives to conventional lead-based perovskites because of their superior environmental compatibility, enhanced chemical stability, and reduced toxicity. In this research study, the performance of a solar cell architecture FTO/IGZO/Cs 2 AgSbCl 6 /Cu 2 O are systematically studied by the simulation software known as SCAPS-1D. DFT calculations were performed using WIEN2k package to investigate structural and optoelectronic properties of Cs 2 AgSbCl 6 material to determine its suitability for photovoltaic applications. Afterwards, the photovoltaic performance is comprehensively studied with respect to the absorber thickness (t active ), bulk defect density (N t ), donor and acceptor concentration (N A and N D ), carrier mobility (u n and u p ), operating temperature (T), illumination intensity (I sun ), series and shunt resistance (R s and R sh ) and contact work functions (WFs). The optimized device shows a higher power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 28.53%, open circuit voltage (V oc ) of ~1.068 V, short circuit current density (J sc ) of 32.81 mA cm −2 and fill factor (FF) of 81.38%, which is found better than the initial device having PCE of 24.77%. The improvement in performance mainly has been attributed to the improvement in energy-band alignment (EBA), efficient extraction of the carriers, suppression of the interfacial recombination, and optimization of the electrical transport through the IGZO/Cs 2 AgSbCl 6 /Cu 2 O heterostructure. In addition, the data set created from the above-mentioned SCAPS-1D simulations was used to train six supervised machine learning algorithms including Linear Regression (LR), Support Vector Regression (SVR), K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), Random Forest (RF), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (xGB), to further accelerate the optimization of the device. The machine-learning analysis accurately estimated the photovoltaic (PV) parameters and defined the major factors that affect the PV performance, such as the carrier mobility, the density of traps, the thickness of the absorber and the illumination intensity.

W7221660704.abstract: Abstract The rapid growth of urbanization has increased the need for intelligent,efficient,and sustainable building design and planning solutions.Traditional building design processes often require significant time,manual effort,and coordination among architects,structural engineers,planners,and other experts. This project,“Smart Autonomous Building Design and Planning Using Generative Multi-AgentSystems, ”proposes an intelligent framework that automates and improves the building design and planning process using Artificial Intelligence(AI) and collaborative multi-agent systems. The proposed system collects input data such as plot dimensions,site information,user require ments,number of rooms, building constraints, environmental conditions,and budget preferences. Multiple specialized AI agents, including a Planning Agent, Architectural Design Agent,Structural Analysis Agent,Sustainability Agent, and Cost Estimation Agent, collaborate to generate and evaluate possible building designs.A Generative AI-based design engine produces optimized floor plans and building layouts based on the collected requirements. The generated designs are evaluated using important parameters such as space utilization,structural feasibility,cost efficiency, energy efficiency,sustainability,and compliance with user-defined constraints.If a generated design does not satisfy the required conditions,the system performs an iterative optimization process to modify the design parameters and generate improved alternatives. The final optimized design can be presented through floorplans and digital visualization. The proposed system aims to reduce manual design effort, improve coordination between different design tasks,and support faster and more intelligent decision-making. By integrating Generative AI with multi-agent collaboration, this project provides a scalable and intelligent approach to ward autonomous, efficient, and sustainable building design and planning.

W7221791055.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in physics research is increasingly common, yet few guidelines exist for its effective use. Starting with a principles-based approach, we outline a set of ten requirements for collaborative AI agents in experimental physics, spanning scientific norms, effective agent use, and domain expertise. We take a human-centered approach in which agents act as collaborators that amplify rather than replace the expertise of a human researcher (user) who directs the work and is responsible for its results. We then present a framework designed to enforce these requirements, detailing methods for improving off-the-shelf behavior of large language models (LLMs) with custom scaffolding and describing general-purpose scientific workflows and skills. In particular, we highlight the power of closed-loop campaigns where agents work iteratively toward a well-defined goal. We demonstrate the potential of this mode of research through six case studies in experimental physics, covering device design, hardware control, neural network optimization, physical model identification, and data analysis. All six case studies result in useful work products that add utility to our research, including a neural network architecture and solid-state quantum defect photodynamic model that substantially outperform our published work; a microwave waveguide design that extends a published design concept to a fabrication-ready device meeting our experimental constraints; a quantum control pulse sequence candidate that improves simulated performance by more than an order of magnitude; commissioning of an NMR spectrometer to $\sim$1~Hz frequency precision on live hardware; and finally a data-fitting pipeline that achieves, to our knowledge, the first reconstruction of the Ising microstate of an artificial spin-ice array from diffraction-limited magnetic imaging.

W7221815149.abstract: Frontier language-model agents can now improve robots on their own: they write control code, test it, and keep what works as skills and memories for the next task. We introduce SEAR (Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics), a framework and benchmark built around two questions. Is the agent really learning, or just trying more often? And does what it learns still help on new tasks, in a new simulator, and on a real robot? The framework runs an agent in three modes: it writes code that becomes the policy (code-as-policy), acts live in the control loop (agent-as-policy), or works as a researcher that fine-tunes a vision-language-action model (auto-research). The benchmark adds controls that separate retained experience from repeated attempts, familiar tasks, privileged simulator state, larger budgets, and luck. Across seven frontier language models, 330 simulated and five physical tasks, and over four years of agent runtime, we highlight three findings. First, the learning curve of a robotic agent depends both on the overall time budget and the task difficulty relative to model capability. Harder tasks make longer sessions worthwhile; on easier tasks, re-rolling short attempts does just as well. Second, control code and shared routines transfer across tasks and simulators, while task-specific solutions do not. On a real robot, we observe a performance gap between agent-designed practice and novel human-designed scenes. Third, different models evolve more effectively in different ways. Some do best acting live, others writing code first. And a text-only model keeps pace with a comparable multimodal one: perception helps with error assessment, but agentic reasoning and tool use can matter more. We release the benchmark and codebase to support future research.

W7221971185.abstract: People delegate multi-step work to LLM agents and read only the reply that the agent hands back. Current evaluation scores task completion and the faithfulness of reports, and it leaves open whether the requester can understand and use the reply. We call this property reply usability and measure it with a reader model that takes the requester's position and tests whether the reply can be interpreted from what the requester has seen, is in the requester's language and answers the request. Its agreement with the majority of five annotators lies within the range of the individual annotators. Across eight models from seven families, 54% of 480 replies fail, and the best model still fails on 30%. Failed replies mostly point to material the requester has not seen or use labels that the agent coined during its work. Stating explicit requirements for the reply reduces the failure rate from 0.52 to 0.43 together with errors and omissions, and a secondary model that rewrites the reply reduces it to 0.36, which human annotators confirm in a blind comparison. Reply usability can thus be scored alongside task success and improved with one appended message or one call to a secondary model.

W7222063452.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a rare and progressive disease associated with substantial clinical heterogeneity and high health care costs. While machine learning (ML) has been increasingly applied to predict clinical outcomes, approaches that integrate clinical prediction with downstream economic modeling remain limited. OBJECTIVE: This study proposes and evaluates an ML-based framework that combines prediction of future functional status with estimation of associated health care costs in patients with PAH. METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study, data from 181 patients with PAH were analyzed. A total of 6 supervised ML algorithms (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator [LASSO] regression, ridge regression, k-nearest neighbors, decision trees, random forest, and gradient boosting) were trained to predict the relative change in World Health Organization functional class (WHO-FC) from baseline to 12-month follow-up using baseline clinical variables. Predicted change rates were subsequently converted to predicted WHO-FC values at the 12-month follow-up for downstream health care cost estimation. Missing values in predictor variables were imputed using median substitution. Median imputation was performed before the dataset was split into training and test sets. Model performance was evaluated using Pearson correlation coefficient (r), and error metrics (RMSE, MAE, and MedAE), based on cross-validation and independent test set validation. Predicted WHO-FC values were subsequently linked to externally validated, stratified real-world health care cost estimates to approximate future economic burden. RESULTS: =0.09). Prediction errors were comparable across models. Estimated mean health care costs ranged from US $12,481 to $12,614 per patient per month. Despite a significant improvement in WHO-FC over 12 months, estimated health care costs remained largely unchanged, reflecting persistent economic burden across functional class strata. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates the feasibility of an ML-based framework that integrates prediction of functional status with health care cost estimation in PAH. While predictive performance was moderate, the approach illustrates how ML models can be extended beyond clinical end points toward system-level applications such as cost forecasting and resource planning. Further validation in larger, multicenter cohorts is required before clinical or health system implementation.

W7222894924.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (STs) measures gene expression while retaining the location of transcripts or cells within tissue sections. Unlike bulk RNA sequencing, which averages expression across cell populations, and single-cell RNA sequencing, which generally requires tissue dissociation, ST links molecular profiles to tissue architecture. This spatial information supports the analysis of tissue heterogeneity, cellular organization, and potential intercellular interactions. The spatially resolved nature of ST has unlocked diverse applications in fields such as cancer, neuroscience, reproductive biology, and plant biology. In parallel, the development of publicly accessible databases and repositories has facilitated large-scale, multi-cohort comparisons and benchmarking. The rapid expansion and increasing complexity of these datasets have driven the adoption of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and artificial intelligence (AI) techniques. These computational tools support a range of tasks, including data pre-processing, image segmentation, spatial domain identification, and pattern recognition. Moreover, they are instrumental in integrative multi-omics analyses and predictive modeling. This AI-focused review provides necessary background on ST technologies and databases and evaluates the use of statistical, ML, and DL methods across the analytical workflow, from image and sequencing-data preprocessing to spatial analysis and LLM-assisted interpretation. We compile key resources related to datasets, AI-driven analytical frameworks, and ST data analysis pipelines, and discuss current challenges, limitations, and future directions for AI-based tools in spatial omics.

W7222901226.abstract: Abstract Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) are in-creasingly being considered for critical applications such as healthcare, finance, cybersecurity, and autonomous transporta-tion. These systems consist of multiple intelligent agents that can independently perceive information, reason about their environment, communicate with other agents, and execute deci-sions. Although multi-agent architectures provide flexibility and scalability, their distributed decision-making process can make the overall system difficult to understand, audit, and verify. Existing Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques such as Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) primarily fo-cus on explaining individual machine-learning predictions. They provide limited support for representing collaborative reasoning, inter-agent communication, conflicts, and collective decisions. This paper proposes an Explainable Decision Graph (EDG) framework for representing the reasoning process of autonomous multi-agent systems in a structured and interpretable form. The proposed framework models agents, observations, evi-dence, communications, intermediate decisions, conflicts, verifi-cation events, and final actions as interconnected graph com-ponents. A verification layer enables decision pathways to be examined against predefined safety and policy constraints. The resulting graph can provide different levels of explanations for end users, developers, and auditors. The paper defines an experimental methodology using multi-agent execution traces and proposes evaluation through ex-planation fidelity, completeness, decision traceability, human comprehensibility, decision accuracy, explanation consistency, and computational overhead. Empirical numerical results are intentionally reserved for the implementation and evaluation stage.

W7222918778.abstract: BACKGROUND Identifying individuals on parole or probation can help inform care pathways and ensure continuity of care in health care systems. However, this sensitive justice-related information is often absent from structured electronic health record fields and is instead documented in narrative clinical notes. Developing automated parole and probation detection (PPD) systems typically requires expert-annotated clinical data, but manual annotation is costly, time-consuming, and constrained by data sparsity and privacy concerns. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to develop and evaluate a synthetic-only training paradigm for PPD from clinical text that eliminates the need for expert-annotated training data while maintaining strong performance and cross-domain transfer to real-world data. METHODS We developed Synth-PPD, a synthetic dataset comprising 7579 labeled clinical notes generated using large language models (LLMs), redundancy filtering, and automated quality evaluation. Dataset quality was assessed through human review of 1517 synthetic notes by 2 annotators. The primary outcome was the macro–F1-score for PPD. We evaluated Synth-PPD across unsupervised and supervised learning settings using LLMs, traditional machine learning models, and transformer encoders. Performance was assessed on 293 expert-annotated real-world clinical notes from the US Department of Veterans Affairs. RESULTS Synth-PPD achieved 90.05% human-LLM alignment. In the unsupervised setting, Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct with chain-of-thought prompting and few-shot examples from Synth-PPD achieved a macro–F1-score of 87.22%, outperforming both the corresponding zero-shot model (80.10%) and the best rule-based baseline (77.55%; P<.001 for all comparisons). In the supervised setting, Llama 3.1-8B fine-tuned on Synth-PPD achieved a macro–F1-score of 81.43%, exceeding the best rule-based baseline (77.55%; P<.001) and achieving a numerically higher score than the substantially larger zero-shot Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct model (80.10%; P=.08). In contrast, traditional machine learning models and transformer encoders exhibited greater performance degradation under domain shift and derived limited benefit from increasing synthetic training data. Additional experiments showed that increasing synthetic training data improved cross-domain performance for LLM-based models but yielded comparatively smaller gains for traditional approaches. CONCLUSIONS Synthetic data generated by LLMs can serve as a scalable, cost-effective, and privacy-preserving alternative to expert-annotated real-world clinical data for PPD from clinical text. The findings demonstrate successful cross-domain transfer to real-world US Department of Veterans Affairs clinical notes.

W7223043997.abstract: The token has become the de facto universal unit of measurement in the large language model (LLM) ecosystem: model pricing is quoted per token, context windows are expressed in tokens, inference throughput is measured in tokens per second, and training corpora are reported in trillions of tokens. Yet the token is not a well-defined measurement unit in the metrological sense—it varies with the tokenizer, the vocabulary, text normalization, and the vendor’s counting convention; it is incommensurable across models; and it lacks calibration, traceability, and an assessable uncertainty. This paper examines token metering as an object of measurement science. We first survey the state of token counting, covering the lineage of tokenization techniques, multilingual and domain disparities, divergent billing conventions, and reproducibility issues, substantiated by a first-hand benchmark across 13 tokenizers and 18 multilingual parallel texts. Drawing on the vocabulary of metrology (the International Vocabulary of Metrology and the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement), we then establish a four-dimensional framework—definiteness, commensurability, traceability, and uncertainty—through which we identify four systemic deficiencies of token counting as a measurement system. We argue that these deficiencies undermine billing fairness, cost comparability, and scientific reproducibility. Finally, we review existing mitigation efforts and outline a standardization agenda spanning technical, metrological, and scholarly-reporting levels. We conclude that token metering currently occupies a “pre-SI” stage of measurement, and that establishing a public reference standard and measurement norms is a prerequisite for the LLM economy and for reproducible LLM science.

W7223061747.abstract: Recent advances in video generative models have enabled flexible conditional generation and editing pipelines, such as text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-guided synthesis. However, these workflows are inherently one-directional, mapping conditions to videos without providing a mechanism to invert this process. In complex media production settings, the ability to recover controllable textual conditions from a given video is highly desirable, yet remains underexplored. While inverse prompting has been studied for image generation, directly extending these approaches to video is challenging due to the need to capture temporal dynamics beyond static appearance, as well as the substantial computational cost of per-video optimization. In this work, we propose the first practical framework for efficient video inverse prompting. Specifically, we formulate inverse prompting as a meta-learning problem and introduce Meta Video Inverse Prompting (MVIP), which learns a meta-prompt optimized over temporal dimensions to enable fast and effective prompt inference. Our approach amortizes the inversion process, eliminating the need for costly iterative optimization at test time. Experimental results demonstrate that MVIP recovers higher-quality inverse prompts with significantly improved reconstruction fidelity compared to image-based inversion and iterative captioning baselines, while achieving substantial gains in efficiency. Code and video results are available at https://ueriniuno.github.io/mvip-page/.

W7223062867.abstract: Large language models, the artificial intelligence (AI) systems behind modern chatbots, are trained on vast amounts of legal text, but can they build on it to write law for situations that text never anticipated? In this study, we analyse AI agents' ability to draft a hypothetical "Constitution" for a "community of AI agents". We design "constitutional assemblies" in which a single language model plays several characters that debate to produce a draft constitution. We find that the assemblies converge on a robust floor of legal provisions, and generate a wide variety of different proposals around it, including several AI-specific provisions with no equivalent in human law. Looking more closely at the "creativity" of these AI agents, we find different levels: most proposals combine existing concepts and themes from human constitutions with AI-specific vocabulary. We introduce a measure of this recombination, which helps identify and highlight the most novel legal material. This study reveals a ceiling on AI creativity: the agents extend familiar legal ideas to new situations, but they do not work through what those situations would change. Although current AI models can help develop new laws, they still depend on human legal reasoning.

W7223122973.abstract: Abstract Background Visual foundation models (VFMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) offer adaptable approaches to neurosurgical imaging, segmentation, intraoperative assistance, and clinical decision support. However, the available evidence varies substantially in model type, supervision, validation setting, and clinical task, and their readiness for routine clinical use remains uncertain. Methods We conducted a narrative review of peer-reviewed primary research reports published between January 2020 and August 2026, identified through PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar. Studies evaluating visual, vision-language, or multimodal foundation models in neurosurgical applications were included. Supervised Vision Transformer (ViT) and ViT–CNN systems were retained as contemporary transformer-based comparator studies but were not classified as foundation models. Evidence was synthesised according to model adaptation, clinical application, within-study comparative performance, validation setting, and translational limitations. Results Seven studies met the review criteria. FastGlioma provided a prospective multicentre evaluation of a visual foundation model for intraoperative detection of glioma infiltration. In lumbar-spine MRI, zero-shot SAM and MedSAM performed below supervised nnU-Net on segmentation metrics. A task-adapted SAM2-UNet system achieved a mean Dice score of 0.771 for brain-tumour segmentation, although its mean IoU was 0.569 compared with 0.571 for Mask R-CNN in the reported comparison. Supervised transformer-based systems demonstrated performance in acute traumatic brain injury triage and vertebral fracture classification, although the latter combined ViT, CNN, ensemble fusion, and GAN-based augmentation. In multimodal reasoning, GPT-4o achieved higher absolute diagnostic accuracy than CNS-Obsidian, whereas CNS-Obsidian had higher length-adjusted diagnostic accuracy. Evidence for clinical translation remained limited by heterogeneous validation settings, incomplete reporting of computational performance and safety outcomes, predominantly single-centre or preclinical evaluations, and limited assessment of patient outcomes. Conclusion Foundation-model-based systems show potential across selected neurosurgical tasks, but current evidence is insufficient to establish routine clinical readiness or patient benefit. Reported results are primarily task-specific and should not be interpreted as evidence of a general architectural advantage. Future studies should evaluate these systems prospectively under human supervision while determining whether clinicians can reliably detect and mitigate erroneous outputs. Multi-centre validation, uncertainty assessment, computational efficiency, workflow integration, and patient-centred outcomes should be prioritised.

W7223125817.abstract: Physics seldom makes breakthroughs when we consider objects only in isolation. Instead we model and measure how objects sit among their neighbours, spatial, temporal, or otherwise: a galaxy in its environment, a halo in its history, a photon hit in a detector. Graphs are ideally suited for encoding exactly these relations, and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) learn the geometric functions that respect them. This review presents the use of GNNs for astrophysics and cosmology, and argues that GNNs often suit physics and physical data better than any alternative: they fit the native geometry of the domain and the signal, enable the incorporation of the symmetries and prior knowledge we already trust and have toiled to build, and stay flexible enough to capture what we do not yet understand. GNNs' physically intuitive workings also render them more interpretable than other deep-learning architectures. We show how we can begin from general principles of the geometry of deep learning and build the graph and the graph neural network from the ground up, and how other architectures, like the convolutional network and the transformer, can be seen as special cases of one unified geometric blueprint. We survey applications across cosmology, galaxy formation, dynamics, and instrumentation; and we chart the frontier. From this survey, we find that only one in six articles outside instrumentation applies GNNs to data rather than just simulations. We also distil a set of best practices, including when not to reach for a graph. Throughout, we will prioritise physical intuition and foundational principles over mathematical machinery whenever possible.

W7223219158.abstract: Background: Cancer screening plays a crucial role in early diagnosis and improved survival, yet conventional screening methods are limited by false-positive findings, false-negative results, interobserver variability, delayed reporting, and unequal access to expert interpretation.Objective: To review recent advances in artificial intelligence-assisted cancer screening, focusing on applications in radiology, histopathology, and liquid biopsy.Methodology: This narrative review summarized published evidence on the role of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning in cancer screening.The review focused on three major domains: AI-assisted radiology, AI-assisted histopathology, and AI-assisted liquid biopsy.Results: AI-assisted radiology has shown value in lesion detection, image classification, risk stratification, and workflow prioritization, particularly in breast and lung cancer screening.In histopathology, AI supports tumor detection, grading, biomarker quantification, margin assessment, and reduction of interobserver variability.In liquid biopsy, AI improves interpretation of circulating tumor DNA, circulating tumor cells, methylation markers, microRNAs, and other molecular biomarkers for early cancer detection and tumor-origin prediction.Conclusion: Artificial intelligence has considerable potential to strengthen cancer screening by improving early detection, diagnostic accuracy, efficiency, and individualized risk assessment.

W7223274917.abstract: —For years, business process automation has depended on Robotic Process Automation (RPA), which performs scripted steps dependably but loses accuracy when documents, layouts or rules shift. Agentic AI replaces the fixed script with a goal-oriented cycle in which a large language model (LLM) plans, invokes tools, inspects what comes back and adjusts. This paper examines that change through a representative back-office task: vendor invoice processing together with query resolution. We (i) survey the literature on agents, tool use, orchestration and benchmarks, (ii) put forward a layered, governance-first architecture built from an orchestrator, narrowly scoped worker agents, a schema-validated tool registry, memory and human-approval gates, (iii) set it against RPA in terms of architecture, performance and cost, and (iv) specify an 80-case evaluation protocol. Figures reported in earlier work show that RPA stays faster, and at least as dependable, on stable tasks, whereas an LLM agent reduced build effort by roughly 4–16× and coped with layout variation. A parametric model calibrated on those figures projects that agents become cheaper than RPA once about 20–30% of volume is non-standard, that token spend accounts for less than 16% of effective cost, and that a hybrid of RPA and an agent is the least expensive option. These projections come from a model rather than from measurement; evaluating the prototype is planned future work.

W7223283305.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can translate natural-language optimization problems into solver programs, but reliably producing correct formulations and implementations remains challenging. Existing approaches improve optimization modeling through agentic workflows or task-specific post-training. This raises a practical question: can a lightweight harness using a single model role achieve competitive performance without additional training? We introduce OPTICYCLE and OPTISTATE, two lightweight inference harnesses for optimization modeling, and evaluate them on nine benchmarks comprising 2,634 problems using 11 Qwen variants spanning 0.6B-27B parameters. Our results show that execution-guided revision consistently improves macro accuracy over direct generation for all evaluated models, with gains of up to 49.46 percentage points. Despite their simplicity, both harnesses outperform six adapted agentic workflows in same-model comparisons and four evaluated post-trained optimization models at comparable model sizes, without additional training. Explicit formulation state provides further but model-dependent improvements, suggesting that additional structure is not universally beneficial.

W7223384930.abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) have emerged as fundamental structures for representing and reasoning over large-scale structured knowledge. This paper presents AdaProp-MRAT (Adaptive Propagation Multi-Relational Attention), a novel framework for knowledge graph representation learning and reasoning using deep learning-based graph neural networks (GNNs). We propose a unified architecture integrating multi-relational graph attention mechanisms with entity-specific adaptive propagation weights, extending prior work on adaptive propagation by combining it with hierarchical attention mechanisms. Our framework achieves Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of 0.386 ± 0.008 on FB15k-237 and 0.501 ± 0.006 on WN18RR. For comparison, established baselines achieve lower performance: CompGCN (0.355, 0.479), R-GCN (0.337, 0.454), and RotatE (0.338, 0.476) on FB15k-237 and WN18RR respectively. While recent state-of-the-art methods such as NBFNet achieve 0.415 MRR on FB15k-237, our approach demonstrates competitive performance with a unique contribution of unifying attention and propagation mechanisms (paired t-test, Bonferroni-corrected, $\mathbf{p}\lt \mathbf{0. 0 0 5}$). Experimental validation across benchmark datasets with multiple runs demonstrates the efficacy of our approach. We provide evidence of convergence properties, computational efficiency, and robustness through comprehensive ablation studies and statistical analysis.

W7223939156.abstract: Organizations are increasingly relying on autonomous agents based on artificial intelligence (AI) to execute everyday business processes.These systems, referred as "Agentic AI", have access to sensitive data and information systems, operating without constant human oversight.This article proposes viewing such agents as a new class of insider threat.It analyzes key attack vectors against these systems, specifically: instruction injection, excessive autonomy, tool misuse, and uncontrolled data exfiltration.The proposed approach for developing information security systems is based on a conceptual model and a UML class diagram, augmented with a new "autonomous agent control" component and an "Action Gateway" class.The latter assesses the risk associated with each agent action, determining whether it should be permitted, escalated to a human for decision making, or blocked.The framework is demonstrated through three attack scenarios within a financial organization, illustrating how the proposed mechanisms can thwart attacks that bypass other security controls in this specific configuration.The framework is compared with similar approaches for controlling agent actions (such as GuardAgent and CaMeL); security is ensured through integration with the organization's existing security architecture, as well as by routing medium-risk actions to a designated responsible individual.

W7224177842.abstract: Autonomous Agentic Finance: AI Agents as On-Chain Market Makers and Liquidity Providers This white paper explores the potential of large language model (LLM)-driven AI agents to support liquidity management in decentralised finance (DeFi), particularly within automated market makers (AMMs). It examines the challenges liquidity providers face, including loss-versus-rebalancing (LVR), impermanent loss, changing market volatility, transaction costs, maximal extractable value (MEV), and the complexity of managing concentrated liquidity positions. The paper introduces the proposed Agentic Liquidity Governance Framework (ALGF), a governance-first architecture that combines AI-assisted interpretation of market signals with deterministic risk controls, transaction validation, execution safeguards, and human oversight. It outlines a five-tier autonomy model, ranging from passive observation to open-ended autonomy, with clearly defined permissions, escalation procedures, audit logs, and criteria for increasing or reducing agent authority. In addition, the paper examines the potential effects of AI-managed liquidity on market depth, price discovery, liquidity concentration, and coordinated market behaviour. It addresses critical risks, including manipulated data, prompt injection, model errors, front-running, and accountability challenges. Finally, it proposes a shadow-mode evaluation protocol to assess agent decisions against passive and rule-based liquidity management strategies before any live deployment. The white paper presents a conceptual framework and research agenda rather than validated trading results. Its central contribution is a governance-oriented approach to exploring how AI agents could participate in on-chain liquidity management while maintaining transparency, enforceable limits, and clear operational accountability.

W7224449821.abstract: ABSTRACT Prostate‐specific membrane antigen (PSMA) is a Type II transmembrane glycoprotein markedly overexpressed on prostate cancer cells, enabling a single molecular target to support both positron emission tomography (PET) imaging and targeted radionuclide therapy. Over the past decade, PSMA‐PET/CT has been incorporated into international guidelines for primary staging of high‐risk prostate cancer and for biochemical recurrence, with the landmark proPSMA trial establishing its diagnostic superiority over conventional imaging; whether PSMA‐PET‐guided management improves long‐term oncologic outcomes, however, remains an open question addressable only by prospective PSMA‐specific trials. On the therapeutic side, 177 Lu‐PSMA‐617 has become a standard treatment option for metastatic castration‐resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) after androgen‐receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI) and taxane chemotherapy, and is moving into earlier lines of disease. Alpha‐emitting and next‐generation ligands, together with quantitative whole‐body imaging and artificial intelligence, are redefining both patient selection and response assessment, although randomized evidence for many of these approaches remains limited. In Japan, the concurrent 2025 approval of 177 Lu‐vipivotide tetraxetan and its companion PSMA diagnostic has initiated a national roll‐out that will depend on a hub‐and‐spoke framework of regional PSMA‐PET centers and therapy spokes, a prepared nuclear medicine workforce, and domestic registries to refine Japanese‐specific evidence. This review summarizes the current clinical evidence for PSMA‐PET/CT and 177 Lu‐PSMA radioligand therapy, highlights interpretive and implementation pitfalls, and outlines practical priorities for the Japanese clinical and academic community.

W7224541812.abstract: Activation steering controls language model behavior at inference time by injecting behaviorrelevant directions into internal representations.In the standard steering interface, a steering direction is estimated once before generation and then applied throughout decoding.However, during multi-step reasoning, the model's internal state shifts continuously as reasoning progresses, while standard steering continues to apply the same fixed direction across these changing states.This creates a mismatch between the model's evolving reasoning state and the static intervention applied to it.To address this mismatch, we introduce State-Conditioned Steering (SCS), which recomputes the additive update itself from the hidden states encountered during generation while keeping the same additive intervention interface.Rather than adapting when or how strongly to intervene, SCS re-estimates the update from intermediate reasoning states as generation proceeds.In a paired comparison setting, we compare fixed and state-conditioned updates and find that predefined directions often exhibit unstable effects, while SCS yields more consistent intervention behavior across decoding steps.Across reasoning benchmarks with explicit step structure and three instruction-tuned backbones, SCS achieves larger average gains than promptingonly decoding and baseline activation steering methods.

W7224650196.abstract: Latent communication provides an efficient alternative to text-based exchange in multi-agent LLM systems by transmitting continuous hidden representations instead of natural-language messages.However, opacity is not privacy: latent messages may still carry private prompts, agent memory, or task-irrelevant sensitive information recoverable by downstream agents or adversaries.We study this risk through communicated latent messages, the edge-level representations that cross agent boundaries and define the privacy interface of latent multi-agent systems.We identify two coupled leakage mechanisms: instantaneous leakage from individual messages and propagation leakage accumulated across multi-round transcripts.We propose Information-Constrained Latent Communication (ICLC), a model-agnostic communication-layer framework that constrains latent information exposure without modifying backbone LLM parameters.ICLC combines a receiver-conditioned latent bottleneck, adversarial regularization over messages and transcripts, and topology-aware gates that suppress unnecessary communication edges.Across private-context question answering, collaborative reasoning, and tool-use planning, ICLC preserves the utility benefit of latent communication while reducing average leakage from 0.747 to 0.398 compared with raw latent communication.These results suggest that privacy in latent multi-agent systems should be treated as a dynamic information-flow problem over messages, edges, and interaction rounds.

W7224781694.abstract: The development of blockchain applications demands expertise across smart contracts, backend services, frontend interfaces, and security auditing, a rare combination that creates barriers to entry and constrains innovation. While existing frameworks attempt to address individual aspects of this complexity, they remain fragmented and require manual integration, leaving developers to navigate disconnected tools without end-to-end automation. More critically, the increasing adoption of AI-assisted coding introduces a risk through homogeneous vulnerability patterns, as developers using similar language models replicate security flaws across multiple applications. To address these challenges, we present VibeDApps, a multi-agent architecture that transforms DApp development from a manual, expertise-intensive process into an orchestrated workflow where four specialized agents, Contract, Backend, Frontend, and Audit, collaborate through structured protocols to generate applications from natural language specifications. Unlike approaches where AI serves merely as a coding assistant, our agents operate as autonomous peers, with each maintaining deep domain expertise while coordinating through asynchronous message passing to ensure system-wide coherence. The architecture's central innovation lies in its generation strategy that combines multiple approaches, including template instantiation, pattern composition, and guided synthesis, specifically designed to avoid the homogeneous vulnerabilities that arise when relying on single-model generation. Furthermore, security validation is embedded continuously throughout the development lifecycle rather than relegated to post-development auditing, enabling immediate detection and correction of vulnerabilities as code is generated. Evaluation across 50 DApp specifications spanning DeFi protocols, NFT marketplaces, and DAO systems shows average generation times of four minutes with high success rates for standard patterns. Complex DeFi protocols with circular dependencies are more challenging but can be improved through dependency resolution algorithms. Statistical validation confirms all performance claims with high confidence. This work lays the foundations for democratizing blockchain development, enabling developers without specialized expertise to create secure DApps while meeting the stringent security requirements of financial applications in adversarial environments.

W7224837958.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as cognitive interfaces that shape how users interpret evidence, communicate, and make decisions. As deployed systems become more multimodal, tool-using, and multi-agent, safety failures no longer arise only from isolated harmful outputs, but also from how agents update, store, and propagate epistemic commitments across retrieval, memory, tools, and peer communication. In this paper, we define belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments that guide downstream action. Building on this view, we propose the Explicit Belief Multi-Agent System (EB-MAS), which externalizes belief states into a structured substrate, uses belief operators to propose candidate updates, and applies a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues. We also discuss the risk of group belief at the group level, including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation, and outline practical integration challenges around grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse. Therefore, scalable agent safety requires not only better output filtering or stronger base models, but also explicit interfaces for tracing, calibrating, and constraining belief revision at runtime.

W7224921898.abstract: The swift expansion of multimodal health data, such as EHRs, medical images, lab reports, physiological signals, and clinical notes, has opened up many avenues for intelligent clinical decision support systems. However, the traditional AI models are generally considered to be black-box systems, which does not equate to clinician’s confidence and ease of use in real-world health care situations. Therefore, this study presents an Agentic Explainable Artificial Intelligence (AXAI) Framework for intelligent clinical decision support by integrating Large Language Models (LLMs), multimodal healthcare data, and autonomous AI agents. The presented framework uses specialized agents intended for data collection, data processing, multimodal feature extraction, explainability generation, and validation of decisions. Structured clinical information is combined with unstructured texts and imaging information to obtain a detailed description the patients. Multimodal fusion is used to combine structured clinical data with unstructured medical text and images. This is done to ensure a full representation of the patient. The reasoning agents use LLMs to give diagnostic suggestions and treatment recommendations based on the available clinical guidelines. Explainable AI methods to provide feature attribution, reasoning based on facts, measurement of confidence, and natural language explanations backing recommendations have been added to the framework to increase reliability and trust of clinicians. In addition, there is an autonomous validation entity responsible for assessing consistency of the decisions-making process, identifying contradictory evidence, and allowing human verification of the system before making recommendations. Experimental tests show that the suggested framework produces better diagnostic accuracy, interpretability, robustness, and decision consistency than traditional clinical decision systems based on machine learning and deep learning. The agentic design also allows for more adaptation to different healthcare scenarios while cutting down on diagnostic uncertainty through the cooperative reasoning of different intelligent agents. The proposed framework introduces a reliable, scalable, and transparent method for innovative intelligent healthcare systems by employing multimodal learning, explainable AI, and autonomous decision-making with LLM to aid healthcare professionals in providing effective, personalized healthcare for patients.

W7224960008.abstract: Despite their strong performance, large language models remain highly sensitive to prompt formulation. This issue is typically addressed at inference-time through manual prompt optimization, which introduces overhead and lacks scalability. Conversely, we focus on train-time approaches that build prompt robustness into the model during instruction tuning. A common strategy is to mix multiple paraphrases of each prompt into training. We demonstrate that across trainable parameters, the per-paraphrasing gradients interfere, with 57% exhibiting sign conflicts and the naive gradient average discarding approximately a fifth of the magnitude. Therefore, we develop two gradient-merging methods, Prompt-TIES and Prompt-DARE, that address this interference by leveraging interference-resolution operators from model and gradient merging and applying them to prompt gradients. In this study, we compare the efficacy of our methods to increase model robustness to train-time robustness methods spanning all three established classes: data construction, consistency regularization, and contrastive alignment. The evaluation is conducted across four models from two families at two scales. We observe the interaction between prompt phrasing and the specific examples accounts for 54% of per-example variability on average, and exceeds 70% on tasks such as ANLI and WiC. The gradient-merging methods directly improve this local robustness and nearly halve per-example variance on fully fine-tuned models at little cost to overall accuracy. The other train-time methods enhance raw performance, but fail to improve per-example variance reliably. Code: https://github.com/FSadrieh/prompt-agnostic-llms. Model checkpoints: https://huggingface.co/prompt-agnostic-language-models.

W7225003736.abstract: Trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI) requires more than technical performance. However, its requirements are often assessed separately, with limited integration across the AI lifecycle. Responsible AI (RAI) concerns the practices and governance applied throughout AI design, development, deployment, use, and monitoring. Trustworthiness describes the properties of an AI application within its sociotechnical context. Explainable AI (XAI) comprises methods that improve the understanding of model behaviour and outputs. Explainability supports trustworthiness but does not replace it. This article proposes a unified concept linking five dimensions of trustworthy AI: technical trustworthiness; transparency and governance; human and social responsibility; ethical and legal alignment; and sustainability and impact. Its main conceptual contribution is the simultaneous consideration of these interdependent dimensions across data, development, validation, deployment, and monitoring. Unlike the Assessment List for Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (ALTAI), Z-Inspection, the Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence Maturity Model (TAIMM), and the Multisource Artificial Intelligence Scorecard Table (MAST), the proposed concept emphasizes cross-dimensional relationships within a common assessment structure. These relationships connect explainability, accountability, fairness, robustness, and safety across the AI lifecycle. The concept provides a basis for coordinated assessment and governance of technical, human, ethical, legal, social, and environmental requirements.

W7225202413.abstract: Clinical EEG interpretation requires integrating technical quality, background and behavioral states, interictal and ictal abnormalities, and overall clinical context across long recordings. We introduce ERIA (EEG Reporting and Instruction-Optimized Agent), a locally deployable framework in which a single 27B language-model controller analyzes whole-recording EEGs by orchestrating specialized parametric and signal-processing tools. ERIA combines learned tools for background abnormality, sleep-wake state, seizure-like activity, and interictal epileptiform discharges with deterministic spectral, amplitude, symmetry, montage, and signal-quality analyses. Rather than fine-tuning the controller or using multi-agent orchestration, ERIA keeps the controller weights, specialist tools, and safety constraints fixed and optimizes only its natural-language analysis policy with GEPA (Genetic-Pareto), using feedback from expert-written EEG reports. GEPA improves physician-aligned whole-recording report quality over the raw policy, and the optimized policy transfers to external EEG benchmarks. On CerebraGloss-Bench and BrainBench Foundational Analysis, ERIA remains competitive with the models evaluated in the original benchmarks. These results show that specialist tools and language-level policy optimization can extend the clinical and general EEG capabilities of a single locally executable model while preserving local inference and traceable tool use.

W7225237461.abstract: The rapid development of large language models, generative artificial intelligence, and multi-agent systems is driving enterprise digital transformation from "system-assisted operation" toward "agent-based collaboration." The widespread application of agents does not merely improve local work efficiency; rather, it will further reshape the organizational structure, decision-making mechanisms, boundary forms, capability systems, and headquarters functions of enterprise groups. Based on organizational design theory, transaction cost theory, and dynamic capabilities theory, this paper reviews the evolutionary process of organizational transformation in enterprise groups and analyzes the trends of organizational transformation in the age of agents. The study finds that organizational transformation in enterprise groups in the age of agents is mainly reflected in the following aspects: organizational structures are shifting from hierarchical bureaucracy to platform-based, networked, and agent-augmented organizations; decision-making mechanisms are moving from experience-driven decision-making to hybrid decision-making that integrates data, algorithms, and managerial judgment; organizational boundaries are evolving from internal group boundaries to data boundaries, algorithmic boundaries, and ecosystem boundaries; organizational capabilities are being upgraded from digital capabilities to agent orchestration capabilities; and enterprise group headquarters are transforming from "control-oriented headquarters" to "intelligent orchestration headquarters."

W7225301940.abstract: Abstract Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate offensive-security tasks, but success on isolated challenges does not establish reliable long-horizon autonomy. We study this distinction in authorized capture-the-flag (CTF) and wargame environments and introduce a planner-directed architecture in which a persistent non-executing planner delegates on demand to transient, context-isolated specialists with retrievable skills, persistent execution, compact memory, guardrails, and configurable model escalation. On all 200 challenges of the NYU CTF Bench test split, the system obtains 41 accepted flags (20.5%) and 29 leak-audited genuine solves (14.5%), against 4 (2.0%) and 3 (1.5%) for a stateful single-agent baseline. Both start from gpt-4o-mini, but only the planner-directed system could escalate to gpt-5-mini, which it did on 199 of 200 challenges and for 72.5% of spend. A controlled architecture-by-escalation experiment over a pre-registered subset of 80 challenges, crossing a resource-matched monolithic agent with the planner under matched budgets, was run in two independent formal passes. M0 solves 4/80 then 3/80, M1 22/80 then 19/80, P0 4/80 then 3/80, and P1 14/80 then 15/80. Pooling the two formal passes with challenge as the repeated unit, a clustered GEE shows a strong escalation effect (OR 8.79, 95% CI 3.39−22.81, $$p = 8\times 10^{-6}$$ p = 8 × 10 - 6 ), no architecture main effect (OR 1.17, $$p = 0.34$$ p = 0.34 ), and a significant architecture-by-escalation interaction (OR 0.53, $$p = 0.005$$ p = 0.005 ). Under the spend-constrained 340-action ceiling, the coordination cost of specialist delegation, context restart, and evidence folding offsets any additional solve-rate advantage from the planner-directed structure. On OverTheWire Bandit, the planner-directed system reaches 30/33 standalone and 24/33 sequentially, compared with 27/33 and 23/33 for the strongest single-agent mini backbone.

W7225339483.abstract: The move from lab demonstrations to designed quantum technology is underway, but the development in hardware, algorithms, error correction and safe communication is uneven. The survey is comprehensive, covering the full stack: superconducting, trapped-ion, neutral-atom, photonic, silicon-spin and topological qubits; Shor, Grover, HHL, VQE, QAOA and quantum machine learning; stabilizer and surface-code error correction; quantum key distribution and post-quantum cryptography; and applications in chemistry, finance, logistics, healthcare and security. Published benchmarks up to 2025 are normalized to common metrics and augmented by reproducible simulations. Surface-code simulations at the circuit level show that the threshold is around 0.7-1.0%, and the error-suppression factor increases from 1.6 to 11 when the physical error rate is reduced from 0.6% to 0.1%. UCCSD-VQE reproduces H₂ precisely but misses chemical accuracy for a stretched H₄ chain (5.2 mHa), and a 48-CNOT compilation fails it already at 0.01% two-qubit error. For MaxCut on 3-regular graphs, the QAOA depth required to beat Goemans-Williamson rounding increases from 4 qubits to 6 qubits. The asymptotic decoy-state BB84 reaches 1.5 Mb s−1 over 100 km, whereas the twin-field protocols beat the repeaterless bound beyond 280 km. So, physical fidelity and fault tolerance are still the limiting factors for broad quantum advantage, not qubit count. These comparisons also inform computational decision-making by relating algorithm selection to solution quality, physical error rates, and resource constraints. They provide a basis for assessing where quantum optimization may complement established classical methods in practical decision-support applications.

W7225398408.abstract: Automated database schema matching is an essential process for integrating heterogeneous databases and enabling consistent data exchange across diverse information systems. Traditional schema matching techniques rely on linguistic, structural, instance-based, and machine learning (ML) approaches, but they often struggle with inconsistent naming conventions, domain-specific terminology, complex relationships, and evolving data structures. New developments in large-scale language models allow for better semantic reasoning and contextual comprehension, which in turn improves the ability to find relationships between database attributes. However, standalone models may produce inconsistent predictions and require additional validation for reliable matching. This paper reviews automated database schema matching using agentic large language models and semantic similarity techniques. It examines fundamental schema matching methods, semantic similarity approaches, automation strategies, and agentic reasoning capabilities, including planning, search, and tool utilization. Existing frameworks, including LLM-Matcher and Matchmaker, are discussed alongside machine learning, multimodal fusion, and explainable matching approaches. The review identifies research gaps in autonomous decision-making, iterative validation, scalability, explainability, and reduced human intervention. Finally, it highlights the need for an integrated framework combining agentic reasoning and semantic similarity to achieve accurate, adaptive, transparent, and efficient schema matching across heterogeneous database environments.

W7225420487.abstract: Bio-inspired robotics in combination with deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has become a paradigm shift for creating adaptive, intelligent and autonomous industrial systems. Bio-inspired robots, inspired by biological organisms like insects, mammals, and water-based organisms, exhibit improved locomotion, flexibility and resilience capabilities in dynamic industrial environments. The key aspect of the incorporation of DRL is the ability to obtain optimal control policies by interacting with a complex and uncertain environment without prior programming. This paper explores how the fields of biologically inspired design and the latest developments in DRL are connected to address some of the industrial automation challenges including real-time decision-making, adaptability, energy-efficiency, fault-tolerance etc. The paper highlights the significance of policy gradient methods, value-based learning, and actor–critic architectures in the context of continuous learning and optimization in robotic systems. Furthermore, it addresses the applications of such systems for manufacturing, logistics, inspection and hazardous applications. Technologies like sensor fusion, digital twins and edge computing enhance their performance and scalability of the system. Finally, the paper outlines some of the existing challenges, such as the computational complexity and safety issues, and suggests future research directions to create safe, scalable, and human-like autonomous industrial robots.

W7225425802.abstract: The issue of early cancer diagnosis is decisive in raising the survival rate of patients and providing them with a therapeutic intervention on time. One of the promising diagnostic devices in cancer screening and monitoring in the early stages is liquid biopsy, which is a minimally invasive method, through which circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), circulating tumor cells (CTCs), and other biomarkers of body fluids are studied. Nevertheless, the multidimensional, heterogeneous, and high-dimensional liquid biopsy data makes the correct interpretation based on the conventional machine learning tools to be very challenging. In this paper, we identify how deep learning structures could be utilized to detect early cancer through liquid biopsy data. Complex neural nets like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and Auto encoders, along with Transformer neural contingents are explored due to their potential to derive non-linear patterns and traditional dependencies and represent features using messages on genomics, proteomic, and metabolomics signals. Also, we address data imbalance, feature selection, and model interpretability strategies to increase the clinical reliability. The presented deep learning models show the possibility of the enhancement of sensitivity and specificity of cancer detection in contrast to the traditional models. This paper is a step towards creating scalable, non-invasive, and accurate diagnostic methods of early cancer detection and precision oncology by combining powerful deep learning models and liquid biopsy analytics.
